Rochester Institute Of Technology Won't Recognize Cannabis Coalition -
Fears It "will encourage dangerous criminal elements."

First, it equates marijuana with "drugs." Obviously, Simone knows that alcohol and tobacco are "drugs," and surely he also knows that "marijuana is a drug, therefore all drugs are marijuana and/or marijuana is all drugs" is a logical fallacy.

Second, it cites the costs of marijuana prohibition to justify it. That is, it explicitly recognizes that marijuana is sold in the same distribution channels with hard drugs by "criminal elements." This is precisely the situation that reformers are trying to end, but it is cited as a reason not to recognize a group that advocates the only way to end it.

Third, it argues that discussing ending marijuana prohibition will encourage the use of marijuana by minors, therefore it would undermine the health of the students even to discuss it. This is one of the most common features of prohibitionist propaganda. They say that "drug" use by children is increasing, not because prohibitionist propaganda disguised as "drug education" is a counterproductive fraud, but rather because anti-prohibitionists criticize prohibition.

Fourth, it argues that organized crime would be encouraged by a discussion of something that would have the effect of putting them out of business. It is also a remarkably naïve view of organized crime. "Golly, Sluggo, the RIT students are criticizing marijuana policy, so let’s go on campus and sell them drugs." "Great idea, Boss! Gee, I had never thought of that!"

Fifth, it explicitly says that official recognition of a group implies that RIT therefore endorses the views of the group, putting the university in the odd position of endorsing the often conflicting views of various common campus groups. That is RIT is presumably both Republican and Democrat, conservative and liberal, etc.

In fairness to President Simone, he really was just doing his job, as in "just following orders." Not that anyone had to order him. That is the beauty of a well-established party line.

Now he is dealing with a difficult situation. He obviously should have simply invoked the mantra of "academic freedom" and let the Cannabis Coalition application slide through. Instead, his letter touched all of the bases of the paradigm supporting marijuana prohibition. To back off will require that he implicitly recognize that it is really non-sense or -- more precisely -- anti-sense.

The term "paradigm shift" is something that he certainly understands. He also knows that being the head of an institution of learning during such a shift is uncomfortable at best.

He just publicly endorsed the political equivalent of alchemy: repeating bad policies over and over and over again will eventually make them work.

The role of the RIT Cannabis Coalition is educational. It is clear that they have their job cut out for them -- and it starts at the top.

Richard Cowan)

From Albert Simone to Shea Gunther (gun@filament.net)
(All emphasis added)

Dear Shea:

This letter is a follow-up to your earlier letter, our meeting last week, and my review of the application of the Rochester Cannabis Club, (Ed. note: The actual name is the "Cannabis Coalition") of which you are president, for official recognition as an RIT student club and eligibility for the services and funding which normally follow recognition.

I have carefully considered the information you and the Club have submitted and the arguments in favor of recognition which you articulated in our meeting. I have decided that I must exercise my inherent power as President of this Institution to deny the Rochester Cannabis Club official recognition as an RIT club.

One of the primary responsibilities delegated to me as President of RIT by the Board of Trustees is the oversight of the campus and learning environment at the Institute. The Board legitimately expects me to take steps to insure that the environment on campus is safe and that is will enable students to successfully pursue their academic and professional goals. Activities which endanger the health and safety of our student body and which are highly likely to cause situations which could inhibit the academic progress of students must not be supported or facilitated by RIT.

In my judgment, the recognition of the Rochester Cannabis Club as an official RIT club will be interpreted by students and the general public as RIT officially condoning the use of drugs on this campus.

You and your fellow club members may not intend this effect, but there is ample evidence from previous experience in this and other campus communities that there will be widespread publicity of university recognition of a club which advocates legalization of marijuana use and that most, if not all, of the publicity will imply that the university condones drug use by its students.

It is also clear that such publicity will encourage the dangerous criminal elements connected with drug consumption in our society to come on the RIT campus and make contacts with students with the intention of selling them illegal drugs.

There is, in my judgment, a very real and present danger, as most recently illustrated by the content and extent of the publicity in the Rochester community which occurred as a result of the filing of the Club’s application for recognition, that the widespread interpretation of club recognition by RIT will be that RIT approves of drug use, and that rather swiftly those involved in the illegal drug distribution system will target their dangerous and illegal activities to students on the RIT campus.

There is no doubt that the drug distribution system is controlled by a very dangerous criminal element in our society- people who shoot other people. The drug distribution system links marijuana with coke, crack, heroin, and other hard drugs.

It is essential to the safety of everyone on this campus that we use every legal means possible to keep the people involved in the drug distribution system off this campus. You may recall that just last year one of our students was shot near campus housing by a non-RIT individual whom the police believed was on campus trying to sell drugs.

As I told you in our meeting, even without official club status, you and the other students involved with the Club are free to continue with the club activities of the Rochester Cannabis Club. The Club and its individual members are free to hold discussions and meetings on campus and to use the RIT bulletin boards, walls, and electronic talk groups. The Club can sponsor lectures as it has done in the past or you can participate in the discussions sponsored by others.

This decision is not about restricting the ability of students to engage in discussions or debates or hold meetings. You are free to do all of these things.

However, you are not free through official club recognition to trade upon the RIT name or use RIT student activity funds because to do so would, in my judgment, put the health and safety of your fellow students at risk by signaling to the criminals who currently distribute and push drugs that RIT condones drug use by students and that they are welcome to peddle their illegal wares on this campus.

I appreciate your willingness to engage in dialogue for a cause in which you believe. I hope that you can understand why this decision is necessary for the sake of the safe environment on this campus which allows you and your fellow students the security to be free to study, think, and discuss issues.

Sincerely,

Albert J. Simone AJSPRO@rit.edu
President, Rochester Institute of Technology
